title: Memoirs
description: Ten short, warm memoir pieces told by different narrators: a summer on a lake, a first job, driving lessons, a move across the country, a teacher, a piano, an old neighborhood, a radio internship, a colt and a volleyball team.
topic: Memories of family, work and growing up

lessons.title: A Summer on the Lake
lessons.summary: A woman remembers the summer she turned ten, spent in a cabin by a lake with her brother.
lessons.text:
The summer I turned ten, my parents rented a small cabin on a lake in the north, and for eight weeks the whole world seemed to belong to my brother Sam and me. I have been back to that lake many times since, but it is the first summer that I remember most clearly.

The cabin stood at the end of a glen, a narrow green valley with a stream running down the middle. At the bottom of the glen, the stream ran into the lake. Behind the cabin lay a wide meadow full of tall grass and wild flowers. Early in the summer, the apple trees at the edge of the meadow were still in blossom, and when the wind blew, the white blossom fell on the grass like snow. Later, small purple flowers appeared everywhere. My mother told me they were violets, and that their soft, deep color was also called violet.

What I loved most were the mornings. Every morning, a thin white cloud lay over the water. My father explained that it was moisture: the lake was warmer than the cold night air, so moisture rose from the water and turned into tiny drops above it. As the sun climbed, the moisture disappeared, and by eight o'clock the lake was clear and blue again.

Our days followed a simple pattern. We swam in the morning, read in the afternoon and walked through the meadow in the evening. Sometimes we would lie in the grass awhile and do nothing at all, which, at ten, felt like a great luxury. "Rest awhile," my mother would say. "The lake isn't going anywhere."

In the middle of the summer, a small carnival came to the nearest town. There was a big wheel that lifted you high above the trees, and a man sold sweet corn from a cart. At one of the games, Sam won a tiny glass bear, which he still keeps on his desk. We went to the carnival three nights in a row.

The best gift of that summer, however, came from my grandfather, who visited in August. He brought an old telescope that he had used as a young man. On the first clear night, he set the telescope up in the meadow and showed us the moon. Through the telescope, it was no longer a flat white circle but a real place, with mountains and deep holes. Never before had I understood how large the sky was.

At the end of August, we drove home. I sat in the back of the car and watched the glen grow smaller behind us. I knew, even then, that I would carry that summer with me for the rest of my life, and I have.

Questions:
Where was the family's cabin?
It stood at the end of a glen, a narrow green valley that ran down to the lake.
What did the writer see in the meadow early in the summer and later?
Early in the summer, she saw white blossom on the apple trees; later, she saw small violet flowers.
What was the white cloud over the lake every morning?
It was moisture that rose from the warm lake into the cold night air.
What did Sam win at the carnival?
He won a tiny glass bear, which he still keeps on his desk.
What did the grandfather show the children through his telescope?
He showed them the moon, which looked like a real place with mountains and deep holes.

lessons.title: My First Job
lessons.summary: A woman remembers working as a waitress at a roadside restaurant when she was sixteen.
lessons.text:
I was sixteen when I got my first job, as a waitress at a small restaurant on the highway outside our town. My father had been unemployed for most of that year, since the factory where he worked had closed, and although my parents never asked me to help, I wanted to bring some money home.

The restaurant belonged to a woman named Rose, who had worked in hospitality for thirty years. On my first morning, she told me what she believed hospitality really meant. "It isn't about the food," she said. "Anybody can fry an egg. Hospitality means that every person who walks through that door feels welcome."

The work was harder than I had expected. I learned to carry three plates on one arm, to fetch coffee before anyone asked for it and to remember which customer liked his toast dry. Whenever Rose called my name, I would run to fetch whatever she needed. By the end of each shift, my feet hurt badly, especially my left heel. Rose told me to buy shoes with a soft heel, and she was right: within a week, the pain was gone.

On Fridays, we served fried cod. The fish arrived fresh from the coast every Thursday night, and the cook, a quiet man named Earl, covered it in a light batter and fried it until it was golden. People drove from three towns away for Rose's Friday cod. Whatever was left at the end of the day, Earl wrapped in foil, and I often carried a warm foil package home to my parents.

Some customers paid in cash, but more and more paid with a debit card, which takes the money straight from your bank account. When our old debit card machine failed, a customer would sometimes rant at me as if I had broken it myself. Rose taught me to listen quietly to a rant, to apologize once and then to fix the problem. Most people, she said, simply want to be heard.

She also taught me about discretion. Many customers came every day and told us about their lives: an illness, a divorce, a son who had lost his job. "What they tell you stays here," Rose said. "Use your discretion." I came to understand that discretion, the ability to know what not to repeat, mattered as much as speed or a good memory.

I worked there for two summers. By the second, my father had found a new job, and the money I earned went into a fund for college. On my last day, Rose hugged me and said, "You were a terrific waitress." Coming from her, terrific was the highest praise. I have had many jobs since, but I still remember her words whenever I welcome a guest into my own home.

Questions:
Why did the writer want a job at sixteen?
Her father was unemployed, and she wanted to bring some money home.
What did Rose believe hospitality meant?
She believed it meant that every person who came through the door felt welcome.
What happened to the cod that was left at the end of the day?
Earl wrapped it in foil, and the writer often took it home to her parents.
How did Rose teach the writer to deal with a customer's rant?
She taught her to listen quietly, apologize once and then fix the problem.
What is discretion, according to the story?
It is the ability to know what not to repeat.

lessons.title: Learning to Drive
lessons.summary: A man remembers the Saturday mornings when his grandfather, a former army driver, taught him to drive.
lessons.text:
When I was fifteen, I got my learner's permit, and my grandfather offered to teach me to drive. My parents were both busy, and besides, nobody in our family had more experience behind the wheel. As a young man, he had served as a driver in an army battalion, and the men in his battalion said he was the best driver they had ever known.

He owned an old blue car with a heavy steering wheel and no radio. Every Saturday morning, he picked me up, drove to an empty parking lot behind the church and moved to the passenger seat.

His method was simple and patient. First, I had to adjust the seat and the mirrors. Then I had to reset the trip counter, a row of small numbers beside the speed dial that showed how far the car had traveled. Because we reset it before every lesson, we could write each lesson's distance in a notebook, in neat columns, the way he did everything.

I was not a natural driver. In the first weeks, I stopped too suddenly, turned too wide and once drove straight over a curb. "Gosh" was all my grandfather said that time. Usually, when I made a mistake, he would simply raise one eyebrow. He rarely spoke; the eyebrow said everything. When I did something well, he would rub his forehead and nod slowly, which was his highest form of praise. I came to watch that eyebrow and that forehead almost as closely as the road.

Once I was ready for real streets, he taught me to look out for pedestrians. "A pedestrian has no metal around him," he said. "You have a car, a seat belt and brakes. A pedestrian has only you." He made me slow down near every school and wait for every pedestrian, even a slow one.

His advice was often sage, and it went beyond driving. One day I took a wrong turn and wanted to turn around in the middle of a busy road. "Some mistakes you can undo," he said, "and some you can't. On the road, it is safer to keep going and undo the mistake at the next corner." I have found that sage advice useful in many places since.

Sometimes, as we drove, he talked about his comrades from the army and their long nights on mountain roads. He still wrote to two of those old comrades every Christmas.

My permit would expire in the spring, so I had to pass my driving test before then. I took the test a week before the permit was due to expire, and I passed. "Gosh," my grandfather said when I showed him the paper, "you might drive better than I do." I knew he was joking, but I also knew he was proud. From then on, I drove him to church every Sunday.

Questions:
Why did the grandfather have so much experience behind the wheel?
As a young man, he had served as a driver in an army battalion.
Why did the writer reset the trip counter before each lesson?
He reset it so that they could write each lesson's distance in a notebook.
What did the grandfather do when the writer made a mistake?
He usually raised one eyebrow and said nothing.
What did the grandfather say about pedestrians?
He said that a pedestrian has no metal around him and has only the driver to protect him.
What did the writer do after he passed his test?
He drove his grandfather to church every Sunday.

lessons.title: Three Thousand Miles
lessons.summary: A woman remembers how her family moved from the East Coast to a city near the Pacific when she was twelve.
lessons.text:
The year I turned twelve, my mother accepted a job on the other side of the country, and our family moved from a small town on the East Coast to a city near the Pacific Ocean. It was a distance of nearly three thousand miles, and for weeks before we left, I thought of little else.

A move of that size requires a great deal of coordination. My mother, who loved order, made a list of every task and fixed it to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a lemon. The lemon magnet was her favorite. Without that coordination, my father said, we would have arrived at an empty house with no lights.

Two days before we left, the packers came. There were three of them, and they worked faster than anyone I had ever seen. The packers wrapped each plate in paper, filled each box tightly and wrote its contents on the side. In one afternoon, the house we had lived in for eight years became a dwelling of empty rooms and echoes. It no longer felt like a home, only a dwelling, and I walked through every room to say goodbye.

We drove across the country in five days. This was before everyone had a smartphone, and my father carried a large cellular phone that worked only near cities, because the cellular network did not yet reach the empty land between them. Inevitably, the phone lost its signal in the middle of the desert, and, just as inevitably, that was where a tire went flat. A truck driver stopped to help us, and within an hour we were moving again.

Much of the trip is a blur to me now: long roads, gas stations and small hotels that all looked the same. Some moments, however, are not a blur at all. I remember my first sight of the mountains, white against a deep blue sky, and the moment the road came over a hill and the ocean appeared below us.

Our new house was smaller than the old one, but it had a lemon tree in the yard, which my mother took as a good sign. The first thing she unpacked was the lemon magnet. The second was the afghan, a soft blanket that my grandmother had knitted in squares of red and cream; in America, a knitted blanket like that is called an afghan. That night, the beds were not yet put together, so we all slept on the living room floor, under the afghan and in our warmest sweaters, because the nights by the ocean were colder than we had expected.

I was sure I would hate our new city. Instead, I made friends within a month. I have moved several times since then, and each time, the afghan is the first thing I unpack.

Questions:
Why did the family move across the country?
The writer's mother accepted a job on the other side of the country.
Where did the mother put her list of tasks?
She fixed it to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a lemon.
What did the packers do?
They wrapped each plate in paper, filled the boxes and wrote the contents on the side.
Why did the cellular phone stop working in the desert?
The cellular network did not yet reach the empty land between the cities.
How did the family sleep on their first night in the new house?
They slept on the living room floor, under the afghan and in their warmest sweaters.

lessons.title: The Teacher Who Changed Everything
lessons.summary: A biologist remembers the high school teacher who taught her how to ask questions and find answers.
lessons.text:
I was a poor student until I was fifteen, when I joined Ms. Patel's biology class. Before that, school had seemed to me a long list of facts to be learned and then forgotten. Ms. Patel changed that, and arguably she changed the direction of my life.

The first thing I noticed about her was her clarity. She never used a difficult word without explaining it, and she never moved on until everyone had understood. In our first lesson, she taught us how scientists name living things. Every plant and animal, she explained, belongs to a genus, a group of closely related species. The lion and the tiger, for example, belong to the same genus. A genus is like a family name, and the species is like a first name. Explained with such clarity, an idea that had always seemed dry suddenly made sense.

What made her truly different, however, was her methodology. Most teachers gave us answers; Ms. Patel gave us questions and showed us how to find the answers ourselves. Her methodology had four steps: observe, ask a question, test an idea and study the results. In the spring, each of us was given one small square of the school garden. Every morning for six weeks, I counted the insects on my square and recorded every occurrence of each kind. A small black beetle that appeared only after rain became my favorite occurrence of all.

She worked with each of us individually. Although there were thirty of us, she met us individually once a week to discuss our progress, and she held us accountable for our own work. If I said I would count my insects on Tuesday, she expected to see the numbers on Wednesday. Being accountable, I discovered, was not a punishment. It was a form of respect.

My breakthrough came in May. When I analyzed my counts, I noticed that the beetles appeared most often near a small pipe at the edge of the garden, where the ground stayed wet. It was hardly a scientific breakthrough, but it was a personal one: for the first time, I had discovered something true on my own.

Ms. Patel also taught us that science is a discourse, a long conversation in which people test and question one another's ideas. At the end of the year, she invited us to join that discourse by presenting our results to the whole school. I was terrified, but I did it.

Today I study insects for a living. Two years ago, I visited Ms. Patel, who has now retired. I told her that I still follow her four steps every day. She smiled and said that the methodology had never really been hers; she had simply given us permission to be curious. Arguably, that is the best gift a teacher can give.

Questions:
What was the first thing the writer noticed about Ms. Patel?
She noticed her clarity: she explained every difficult word.
What is a genus, according to Ms. Patel?
It is a group of closely related species, like a family name.
What were the four steps of Ms. Patel's methodology?
They were to observe, ask a question, test an idea and study the results.
Why did Ms. Patel meet her students individually?
She met them individually to discuss their progress and to hold them accountable for their work.
What was the writer's breakthrough?
When she analyzed her counts, she found that the beetles appeared most often where the ground stayed wet.

lessons.title: The Piano
lessons.summary: A man remembers the day his family bought a secondhand piano and carried it home.
lessons.text:
For most of my childhood, my parents promised that we would buy a piano "someday." Until then, our music at home came from an old record player and a single compilation of piano music, a record with twenty short pieces. I played that compilation so often that the needle wore a deep groove into my favorite piece, and the music jumped whenever it reached that groove.

When I was nine, my mother finally found a piano for sale in the local newspaper. The advertisement described it as "almost new," which turned out to be misleading. The piano was nearly fifty years old. Its owner, an elderly man named Mr. Novak, explained that he had repaired it himself after his wife died, and that "almost new" meant he had replaced almost every part himself. It was misleading, but in its way it was also true.

The piano was black and shiny, so shiny that I could see my face in it. Mr. Novak lifted the lid, and I saw the rows of small hammers and long metal strings inside. He pressed a key and showed me how a hammer struck a string. Then he pressed the middle pedal and explained that it worked as a mute: it placed a strip of cloth between the hammers and the strings, so that you could practice at night without waking anyone. "With the mute on," he said, "only you and the piano will hear your mistakes."

Moving it home became a family saga. My father and two uncles carried the piano down Mr. Novak's front steps, across his lawn, into a rented truck and then up the four steps of our house. At one point it stuck in our front door for twenty minutes, while my mother gave advice that nobody followed. The saga of the piano and the door is still told at every family dinner, and every year it grows a little longer.

That evening, the piano stood in our living room, shiny and silent. My mother closed the lid carefully, and then she opened it again, because none of us could stop looking at it.

Learning to play turned out to be time-consuming. For several years, I practiced for an hour every afternoon. It was time-consuming, and sometimes it was boring, but it was also the first thing in my life that I had chosen for myself.

Years later, when I moved into my first apartment, my parents gave me the piano. It is not as shiny as it once was, and there is a small scratch on the lid from the day it stuck in our door. I would not repair that scratch for anything. Sometimes, when I play, I still remember the old record, and the place where the music jumped.

Questions:
Where did the family's music come from before they had a piano?
It came from an old record player and a compilation of piano music.
Why was the advertisement misleading?
It described the piano as "almost new," but the piano was nearly fifty years old.
How does the mute on the piano work?
It places a strip of cloth between the hammers and the strings, so the sound is much softer.
What is the family saga about?
It is about carrying the piano home and the twenty minutes when it stuck in the front door.
Why will the writer not repair the scratch on the lid?
The scratch reminds him of the day the piano stuck in the door.

lessons.title: The Old Neighborhood
lessons.summary: A woman returns to the neighborhood she left as a teenager and sees what has changed and what has stayed.
lessons.text:
Last spring, after almost twenty-five years away, I went back to the neighborhood where I grew up. My family left it when I was 14, the year after a destructive flood filled the lower streets with brown water. Many families, including mine, decided not to stay.

I had expected to find a neighborhood still suffering from the adverse effects of the flood: empty shops, broken windows, few people. Instead, the streets were full, the trees were tall, and the old brick houses had been painted in bright colors.

On the corner of my old street, I met an elderly woman who was sweeping the sidewalk. When I told her who I was, she remembered my parents at once. She explained that after the flood, the residents had formed a small advocacy group. For ten years, that advocacy was patient and steady. The group wrote letters and spoke at city meetings, and it finally persuaded the city to build new walls along the river. Their advocacy also saved the old houses. The city made the historic streets exempt from new building plans. Because the street was exempt, she said, it still looked the way I remembered it.

The city had also decided to prohibit cars on Main Street. "They prohibit cars from eight in the morning until midnight," the woman told me. "At first, everyone complained. Now everyone walks." Children were riding bicycles in the middle of the road where I had once waited for traffic.

The bakery where my mother bought our bread had closed after the flood, but a young couple had decided to reopen it. When they reopen a place like that, the woman said, they bring back more than bread. A small sign in the window said that the bakery accepted cryptocurrency, a kind of digital money. I doubt that many customers pay with cryptocurrency, but the sign made me smile: the old bakery had entered a new century.

In the library, a room was full of objects from the neighborhood's past: tools, letters, old photographs. One artifact was a photo of my fourth-grade class, and there I was, in the second row, with a missing front tooth. I stood in front of that artifact for a long time.

Finally, I walked to our old house. A family was eating lunch in the backyard, under the apple tree my father had planted. I did not knock; I only watched from the gate. The backyard looked smaller than I remembered, but the tree had grown much taller.

On the train home, I unfolded the map the woman had given me and marked our old street. I have since watched the neighborhood's new life unfold from far away, through the advocacy group's letters. I plan to return in the summer, and this time, I will not wait twenty-five years.

Questions:
Why did the writer's family leave the neighborhood?
They left after a destructive flood filled the lower streets with water.
What did the residents' advocacy group do?
It wrote letters, spoke at city meetings and persuaded the city to build walls and protect the old houses.
What does the city prohibit on Main Street?
It prohibits cars from eight in the morning until midnight.
What did the writer find in the library?
She found an artifact from her own past: a photo of her fourth-grade class.
What had the writer expected to find in the neighborhood?
She had expected a neighborhood still suffering from the adverse effects of the flood.

lessons.title: A Summer on the Radio
lessons.summary: A man remembers his summer as an intern at a small radio station and the presenter who taught him.
lessons.text:
In the summer after my first year of college, I worked as an intern at a small radio station in our town. The station had only two studios and nine employees, and the intern, I quickly learned, did everything that nobody else had time to do.

The station's most famous voice belonged to Dolores Grant, the presenter of the morning show. She had been the morning presenter for thirty-one years, and half the town woke up to her voice. On my first day, she shook my hand and said, "An intern is not a servant. An intern is a student. Ask me anything."

So I asked. I asked how she chose her guests, how she prepared her questions and how she stayed calm when a guest said nothing at all. She answered every question, often while she ate. Her days were so busy that she would snatch a sandwich between interviews, or snatch five minutes of sleep on the office sofa. I learned to snatch my lunch in the same way.

One of my jobs was to sort the letters that listeners sent to the station. Dolores warned me that some of them were confidential. People wrote to her about illness, sadness or trouble in their families, and they trusted her not to share their words on the radio. "If a letter is confidential," she said, "it stays in this box, and in your head."

On Friday nights, the station played a program of supernatural stories. Listeners called in to describe strange lights, old houses and visits from ghosts. Dolores did not believe in the supernatural herself, but she loved the program. "People don't really call to talk about ghosts," she told me. "They call because they want someone to listen to them." I sat beside the phone every Friday, writing down the supernatural tales of farmers, nurses and children.

Near the end of the summer, I asked Dolores how she had achieved such advancement in her career, from typing letters to being the station's best-known voice. She laughed. "Advancement," she said, "comes from being curious and showing up on time. Mostly showing up on time."

On my last day, Dolores announced that she would retire at the end of the year. In her final weeks, she trained a young presenter named Maya to take over the morning show. Dolores called it passing the torch, like runners who pass a burning torch from hand to hand in a long race. When she gave Maya the keys to the studio, the whole station gathered to watch the torch being passed.

I never became a presenter myself; I became a teacher. Still, I begin every school year the way Dolores began my summer. "Ask me anything," I tell my students, and most of them do.

Questions:
Where did the writer work as an intern?
He worked as an intern at a small radio station in his town.
How did Dolores describe an intern?
She said an intern is not a servant but a student.
Why were some of the listeners' letters confidential?
People wrote about illness, sadness or family trouble and trusted Dolores not to share their words.
Why did people call in to the program of supernatural stories, according to Dolores?
She thought they called because they wanted someone to listen to them.
What did "passing the torch" mean at the radio station?
It meant that Dolores trained Maya to take over the morning show.

lessons.title: The Colt
lessons.summary: A woman remembers the summer she spent on her aunt's horse farm and the birth of a colt.
lessons.text:
When I was eleven, I spent the summer on my aunt Ruth's horse farm in the hills. Ruth had no children of her own, and I was her only niece, so she called me "my favorite niece" in a voice that made both of us laugh.

The farm had been in our family for more than a hundred years. Ruth's great-grandfather had ridden in the cavalry, the part of an army in which soldiers ride into battle on horses. When he came home, he bought the land with his savings and brought two cavalry horses with him. Every horse on the farm, Ruth told me proudly, came from those two cavalry horses.

There were also cats in the barn, mostly strays that had wandered in from the road. Ruth fed every stray that arrived, and one of them, a thin gray cat, followed me everywhere that summer.

In the second week of July, one of the mares gave birth. Ruth woke me at four in the morning, and we stood in the barn with a lamp while a wet, brown colt slid into the straw. Within an hour, the colt was standing on four long, shaking legs. Ruth let me choose his name, and I called him Pepper.

For a month, I visited the colt every morning. I learned to brush him, to lead him with a soft rope and to stand where he could see me. Ruth explained that a horse is a powerful animal that is easily frightened. "A frightened horse can inflict a serious injury without meaning to," she said. "He can inflict a kick before he even knows you are there."

One afternoon, Pepper ran along the fence and caught his leg on a loose strand of wire. When I reached him, his leg had begun to bleed, and I was terrified. Ruth arrived quickly. She calmed the colt with her voice, cleaned the cut with water and pressed a cloth against it until it stopped bleeding. "A small cut will bleed a lot," she told me. "That doesn't always mean it's serious." Then she walked the entire fence with me, and we removed every loose strand of wire we could find.

Within two weeks, Pepper's leg had healed, leaving only a thin white line. By the end of the summer, he would come to the gate as soon as he heard my voice.

I returned to the farm every summer until I finished school. Pepper grew into a tall, gentle horse, and the gray stray cat grew fat and lazy in the barn. Ruth is old now, and the farm belongs to me. This morning, a new colt was born, and the first person I called was my aunt.

Questions:
Why did Ruth call the writer her favorite niece?
The writer was her only niece, and the joke made them both laugh.
What is the cavalry?
It is the part of an army in which soldiers ride into battle on horses.
What did the writer name the colt?
She named him Pepper.
What did Ruth say a frightened horse can do?
She said a frightened horse can inflict a serious injury without meaning to.
What did Ruth do after the colt's leg began to bleed?
She calmed him, cleaned the cut and pressed a cloth against it until it stopped bleeding.

lessons.title: The Team That Kept Playing
lessons.summary: A woman remembers her high school volleyball team and its old coach, and a game played many years later.
lessons.text:
In high school, I played on a volleyball team that almost never won. We were a small school in a farming town, and most of the girls on the team had never touched a volleyball before they joined. Our coach, Mrs. Ellis, was a math teacher who had played volleyball in college and who believed, against all evidence, that we could be good.

Our greatest rivalry was with the school across the river. The rivalry was older than any of us; our parents had played against their parents, and nobody in town could remember the last time we had beaten them. Every autumn, the game between our two schools filled the gym, and for one night, even people who did not care about volleyball cared about the rivalry.

Usually, however, we played in front of very few people. At most games, there was perhaps one spectator for each player, and the most faithful spectator was Mrs. Ellis's husband, who sat in the top row with a newspaper and never missed a point. Mrs. Ellis taught us to clap for each other after every point, whether we had won it or lost it. "You clap for effort," she said, "not for the score." At first we felt silly, but by the end of the season, the clapping had become a habit, and it made us feel like a team.

In my last year, something changed. We began to win a few games, and then a few more. In November, we played the school across the river, and we won in five long sets. The gym was louder than I had ever heard it. Every spectator was on their feet, and even our opponents began to clap at the end. Mrs. Ellis did not cheer. She sat on the bench, put her hands over her face and smiled.

Many years later, a message reached me from an old teammate. Mrs. Ellis was about to turn seventy, and the school was organizing a game for the alumni of all her teams. I flew home for it. About sixty alumni came, women from many different years, some of them grandmothers, all of them wearing our old blue shirts.

We were slower than we used to be, and nobody kept the score very carefully. But after every point, all of us clapped, just as she had taught us. At the end of the game, the alumni gathered around Mrs. Ellis, now seventy and still standing very straight, and gave her a ball that every one of us had signed.

She held the ball for a long moment. Then she said, "You see? I told you that you could be good." This time, she was the one who began to clap.

Questions:
Why did the team almost never win?
It was a small school, and most of the girls had never played volleyball before they joined.
How old was the rivalry with the school across the river?
It was older than any of the players; their parents had played against each other.
Why did Mrs. Ellis teach the players to clap after every point?
She believed they should clap for effort, not for the score.
What happened in November of the writer's last year?
The team beat the school across the river in five long sets.
Why did the alumni come back many years later?
They came for a game in honor of Mrs. Ellis, who was about to turn seventy.
